key_figures.quote: The Norwegian State Mapping Authority (Statens Kartverk) has estimated the coastline—islands and fjords included—to be 83,000 kilometers: one and a half times the length of the equator (Sandbæk, 2003).
key_figures.statement: A cited estimate puts Norway’s coastline, including islands and fjords, at 83,000 kilometers; this is a figure cited by the authors, not their own measurement.

key_figures.quote: Although directly aquaculture consumes only 0.2 percent of the sea surface within the base line (Ministry of the Environment, White Paper No. 43 [1998–99, ch. 8.1.3]), there are great regional variation.
key_figures.statement: A cited Norwegian government estimate says aquaculture directly occupied 0.2 percent of sea surface within the baseline; this is a cited figure, not the authors’ own finding.

key_figures.quote: Roger Bennett’s observations, after evaluating coastal zone planning processes in 18 Norwegian municipalities, illustrate this well.
key_figures.statement: A cited study evaluated coastal zone planning processes in 18 Norwegian municipalities; this is Bennett’s study, not the authors’ own evaluation.

key_figures.quote: Thus, as in other countries, coastal zone management in Norway is in an ongoing learning phase. In some municipalities, it has taken many years to develop a management plan, as agreement among the affected stakeholders has been impossible to attain.
key_figures.statement: The authors describe some Norwegian municipalities as taking many years to develop a management plan, without specifying a duration or a count of municipalities.

key_figures.quote: It is a recent phenomenon, no more than 20 years old, and still a task that many coastal municipalities have just commenced.
key_figures.statement: The authors characterize Norwegian coastal zone management as no more than 20 years old at the time of writing.

key_figures.quote: For the last 20 years or so it has become one of the most prominent growth industries in Norway.
key_figures.statement: The authors say aquaculture had become one of Norway’s most prominent growth industries over the last 20 years or so; this is their characterization of the industry.

key_figures.quote: For this and other reasons, trawlers in Norway are banned inside the twelve-mile limit.
key_figures.statement: The authors state that Norwegian trawlers are banned inside the twelve-mile limit; this is a legal-policy statement in the article.

key_figures.quote: As an illustration, the Geological Survey of Norway has proposed a development project for coastal mapping (MAREANO), partly based on the premise that our knowledge of the surface of Mars has a resolution 100 times greater than that of our seabed topography
key_figures.statement: The authors cite a comparison claiming that knowledge of Mars’s surface had 100 times greater resolution than Norway’s seabed topography; this is a cited premise for a proposed mapping project.

pq_notes.A0: The authors argue that aquaculture siting and development are shaped by local conditions, available space, existing uses, security-zone requirements, and the planning system. They describe Norwegian coastal planning as primarily municipal, while sector authorities can veto municipal plans when their mandates are affected. A cited government estimate says aquaculture directly consumes only 0.2 percent of sea surface within the baseline, but the authors stress that regional variation and existing zoning can leave little room for additional pens. They argue that space is not effectively unlimited: development can interfere with human and non-human uses, and adding new activities may become a zero-sum game. Their policy argument is for mapping uses, anticipating conflicts, and coordinating activities rather than assuming spatial separation alone will resolve them.
pq_notes.A1: The authors identify site availability as context-dependent: coastal areas differ in natural, social, and cultural conditions, while existing activities, plans, and projects constrain what locations are suitable. They note that demands for security zones and alternative locations make aquaculture space-consuming, and that zoning may leave little room for additional pens in some areas despite low direct occupation nationally. In Norway, the government required coastal zone plans as a condition for new fish-farming licenses, although that requirement was softened to a strong recommendation after political protests. Municipal planning interacts with sectoral rules and authorities, including fisheries, environment, farming, harbor, defense, and veterinary agencies. The authors discuss environmental risk and incomplete knowledge generally, but do not specifically address fish health or disease in siting decisions.
pq_notes.A2: The segment does not describe a step-by-step aquaculture site application procedure or report application-level outcomes. It says that, as a condition for obtaining new fish-farming licenses, the government required municipalities to develop coastal zone plans; the requirement was later softened after political protests but remained a strong recommendation. Municipalities hold primary coastal planning authority, in collaboration with state agencies and stakeholders, but sector authorities may veto plans that conflict with their mandates. If agencies cannot agree, arbitration may follow and can be time-consuming and antagonizing, disrupting local motivation. The authors also report that some municipalities have taken many years to develop plans because stakeholder agreement was impossible, and that some gave up and proceeded case by case. These observations concern planning and coordination, not measured frequencies of application delays or rejections.
pq_notes.A3: The authors do not describe a formal cumulative-effect assessment method for aquaculture production or show how such assessments determine site choices. They argue more generally that coastal ecosystems and social systems are interactive, multiscale, dynamic, and difficult to predict, and that new activity can interfere with existing human or non-human uses. They call for detailed mapping of resources, activities, and actual and potential uses, including sporadic and seasonal uses, to identify stakeholders and risks before conflict. The segment notes that no comprehensive GIS database of coastal areas, resources, or actual and potential uses then existed in Norway. It also argues that planners need both broad, low-resolution knowledge and location- and time-specific high-resolution knowledge. The authors caution that knowledge is incomplete, politically contested, and costly to acquire; no aquaculture-specific cumulative assessment framework is provided.
pq_notes.A5: The authors argue that spatial planning requires multidisciplinary science and informal local knowledge because no discipline or scientific evidence base alone provides all necessary answers. They distinguish broad, low-resolution knowledge, such as trends in fish stocks, from high-resolution knowledge about particular habitats and localities. Planners also need information on user groups, industry trends, suitable and occupied locations, and proposed projects. They warn that information overload and the rising cost of acquiring ecosystem knowledge can limit its usefulness, and that knowledge is not neutral: stakeholders may select evidence that supports their interests. The segment reports that no comprehensive GIS database of Norwegian coastal areas, resources, and actual and potential uses existed at the time. It mentions the proposed MAREANO coastal-mapping project and electronic navigational chart mapping, but does not assess how emerging technology would change aquaculture impacts or siting opportunities.
pq_notes.A6: The authors identify conflicts between aquaculture and other coastal interests as part of wider competition for space among industry, recreation, fisheries, and other uses. They argue that conflict is worsened by treating space as unlimited, assuming boundaries alone will secure peaceful coexistence, and postponing hard choices. In Norway, municipalities’ territorial planning authority is constrained by sector agencies that may veto plans; arbitration can be time-consuming and antagonizing. The authors recommend early stakeholder involvement, transparent and flexible partnerships, mapping existing and seasonal uses, and building cooperative relations and trust. Citing Cicin-Sain and Knecht, they note that early input can complicate and delay planning, but involving users late risks their opposing the whole process. They also caution that participation is not always effective where conflicts or stakeholder numbers are too great, so legitimate management must balance participation with decision-making effectiveness.
pq_notes.A7: The authors do not identify specific measures that aquaculture companies themselves have adopted to improve spatial efficiency or sustainability. Their general recommendations for coastal management include mapping existing, potential, seasonal, and sporadic uses before development; identifying suitable and available locations; and seeking cooperative or symbiotic relations among activities rather than merely separating them. They argue that fisheries, aquaculture, and tourism could potentially support one another, but say Norwegian fisheries and aquaculture management is not targeted at creating such symbioses and is framed by sectoral rather than territorial perspectives. They call for horizontal institutional integration, joint ventures, networks, and partnerships. These are the authors’ proposals for management and coordination, not evidence of industry self-regulation or demonstrated industry measures.
